entry.evidence: it becomes important to find an optimum duration for the input data that can provide a reliable and statistically significant estimate

sequences.source_document: Published paper (publisher XML text; PDF for figure pages)

steps.action: Took from traditional EEW literature the regularity that magnitude-estimate accuracy increases with the duration of P-wave data used.
steps.quote: The accuracy of such estimates has been shown to increase with the duration of data used to calculate them

steps.action: Posed the question of the optimum (minimum) input duration for reliable rapid magnitude characterisation with deep learning.
steps.quote: it becomes important to find an optimum duration for the input data

steps.action: Designed the test as a three-class single-station waveform classifier (noise, low, high magnitude, boundary ML 5.0) evaluated at different input lengths.
steps.quote: Here a local magnitude of 5.0 is taken to be the boundary between the low-magnitude and high-magnitude classes.

steps.action: Varied the decision boundary to magnitudes 3 and 4 and found similar accuracy, precision and recall.
steps.quote: Magnitudes of 3 and 4 were also experimented with as decision boundaries

steps.action: Selected STEAD traces with ML magnitudes and SNR at least 10 dB, split them 60:10:30 into non-overlapping sets by event and station, and cut windows of 1, 3, 10, 20 and 30 s after P arrival with 2.8-3.0 s of pre-signal noise.
steps.quote: We divide the noise and earthquake traces into training, validation and test sets in the ratio 60 : 10 : 30

steps.action: Built the classifier: resampled and augmented the data against a 3300:1 class imbalance, set class weights 1:1:10, used mixed instruments without normalisation, and trained a CNN plus bi-LSTM with Adam, early stopping and learning-rate decay.
steps.quote: To tackle this imbalance problem, we apply resampling of the data (Krawczyk, 2016) as follows.

steps.action: Fixed accuracy, precision and recall, computed from TP/TN/FP/FN, as the evaluation metrics.
steps.quote: we use the metrics listed below to evaluate the model performance

steps.action: Compared softmax outputs with labels for example waveforms from each class, all correctly classified.
steps.quote: In each case the highest probability is predicted for the corresponding class.

steps.action: Compared softmax probabilities for one M2.8 waveform and test-set accuracy, precision and recall across the five input durations; found no systematic dependence on length.
steps.quote: the predicted probabilities are different and show no dependence on the length of input data

steps.action: Retrained the 3 s model five times on the same data, with no fixed random seed, to measure the initialisation randomness as a baseline.
steps.quote: we also looked at the randomness in the performance when the model is trained on the same data five times

steps.action: Kept the claim that variation due to input length is no larger than retraining randomness.
steps.quote: the variation in the results caused by changing the length of data is comparable to the randomness in the results

steps.action: Examined the confusion matrix and the misclassification by magnitude for the 3 s model: errors concentrate near M5.0 and lean towards false high-magnitude calls because of the class weights.
steps.quote: this is intentional as a missed alarm is considered more dangerous than a false alarm in this context

steps.action: Checked classification across hypocentral distance and SNR to show the model does not simply map amplitude or SNR to magnitude; noted noise misclassifications below 20 dB.
steps.quote: there are instances of correct classification across a wide-range of hypocentral distances and signal-to-noise ratios

steps.action: Attributed the residual misclassifications within 5.0 ± 0.5 to label uncertainty in catalogue magnitudes rather than to the model.
steps.quote: even magnitudes of the same scale reported by different agencies can vary by as much as 0.5 magnitude units

steps.action: Proposed, without performing it, recasting the task as regression in a future version.
steps.quote: it might be helpful to treat this as a regression problem instead of classification

steps.action: Compared the overall accuracy (90.04-93.86 %) with the 93.67 % of a published three-station classifier.
steps.quote: comparable to the magnitude classification accuracy of 93.67 % achieved by Saad et al. (2020)

steps.action: Concluded that input length (1-30 s) has no significant effect and characterised the classifier's accuracy and its bias towards the high-magnitude class above M4.5.
steps.quote: has no significant effect on the model performance

tree.answer: Does P-wave input length affect deep-learning magnitude classification?
Yes: performance metrics measured directly on held-out test data
Characterise a single-station classifier and its sensitivity to input length
Implicit only: accuracy grows with length (traditional EEW) versus no effect
Set: input length varied computationally at 1, 3, 10, 20, 30 s
Length effect within retraining noise; boundary, distance and SNR checks
Kept: length has no significant effect; accuracy up to 93.86 %
Survived review with added boundary tests and distance/SNR analysis

end.claim: A single-station CNN plus bi-LSTM three-class magnitude classifier reaches 90.04-93.86 % accuracy, and changing the input length from 1 to 30 s after P arrival has no significant effect on its performance beyond retraining randomness.

decisive_move.sentence: Retraining the 3 s model five times on the same data supplied the randomness baseline against which the length-induced variation was judged negligible; without it the no-effect claim has no reference.

gates.evidence: The question about input length set the five durations tested, but no hypothesis was stated. The no-effect claim could have failed had the length-induced variation exceeded the retraining spread, but the comparison is visual, rests on five retrainings of the 3 s case only, and uses no statistical test. Nothing was fixed in advance: the class weights were 'chosen experimentally' and the M5.0 boundary was 'arbitrarily chosen'.

imports.item: 1D convolutional and bidirectional LSTM network architecture with dropout, max-pooling and softmax
Adam optimiser, categorical cross-entropy loss, early stopping
Resampling and class weighting for imbalanced data (Batista et al. 2004; Krawczyk 2016)
Data augmentation by window shifting and polarity flipping
Accuracy, precision, recall metrics and the confusion matrix

limits: The author responses (AC1, AC2) are empty in the record, so which revisions answered which comments is inferred from comparing the preprint (RC1 supplement) with the final text; RC1's specific comments sit in an annotated manuscript that is not reproduced. The no-effect claim rests on visual comparison of single runs per duration against five retrainings of the 3 s case only; no retraining spread is shown for other durations and no statistical test is reported. Fig. 5 uses one waveform. The boundary tests at M3 and M4 are reported without numbers. No large boundary (for example M7) was tested, as a referee suggested. The held-out test set comes from the same global dataset; no independent region or catalogue is used. Sub-claims: the accuracy range of 90.04-93.86 % (estimate_with_resolution, though the spread across runs is not stated as an uncertainty); most events above M4.5 are classified as high magnitude because of the class weights (regularity_in_range, from one 3 s model); the classifier works across wide ranges of hypocentral distance and SNR (capability_characterized, qualitative). The composition is none_fits because this is a method-sensitivity study: a capability is built, then an input parameter is varied against a retraining-noise baseline, with no stated rivals and no phenomenon to establish.

disagreements.target: Traditional EEW findings that estimate accuracy increases with data duration (Ziv, 2014)
disagreements.support: For the deep-learning classifier, metrics across 1-30 s inputs vary no more than across five retrainings of the 3 s model.
disagreements.quote: changing the length of the waveform (1, 3, 10, 20 or 30 s after P arrival) has no significant effect on the model performance

disagreements.target: Saad et al. (2020) three-station deep-learning parameter classification
disagreements.support: A single-station model reaches accuracy (up to 93.86 %) comparable to the 93.67 % of the three-station approach.
disagreements.quote: Unlike Saad et al. (2020), who use data from three seismic stations to characterise different earthquake parameters

disagreements.target: Lomax et al. (2019) single-station CNN with normalised input
disagreements.support: The paper states the choice not to normalise data and gives no comparison.
disagreements.quote: Unlike Lomax et al. (2019) we do not normalise the data.
